prompt: Why did the SHA-256 sent beside the payment notice fail to protect it?

choices.text: SHA-256 is too weak for JSON
choices.why: The hash worked; it had no key.

choices.text: Whoever changed the body recomputed the hash too
choices.why: Right: a hash has no key.

choices.text: The digest was too short to cover the amount field
choices.why: The digest covers every byte.

choices.text: JSON cannot be hashed reliably
choices.why: Bytes are bytes.

prompt: The gateway and Vereda share a secret key. What can't an HMAC between them prove to a court?

choices.text: That the message was not altered in transit
choices.why: It proves that, to whoever holds the key.

choices.text: Which of the two produced it
choices.why: Right: either could have; no non-repudiation.

choices.text: That the key was 256 bits long
choices.why: Key length is not what a court asks.

choices.text: When the message was received
choices.why: Neither proves receipt time.

prompt: What does an attacker who changes the amount to 120 need in order to produce a valid HMAC tag?
hint: The third capture used the wrong one.

choices.text: Only the new body
choices.why: The body alone gives any tag but the right one.

choices.text: The old tag and the new body
choices.why: The old tag does not help with a new body.

choices.text: The shared key
choices.why: Right: without it there is no way to the right tag.

choices.text: Vereda's TLS certificate
choices.why: TLS has nothing to do with this tag.

prompt: Why is SHA-256(key + message) not a safe substitute for HMAC-SHA256?

choices.text: The key would appear in the output
choices.why: The output is a digest; the key does not appear.

choices.text: SHA-256 cannot take inputs longer than its block
choices.why: It takes any length.

choices.text: It allows length extension
choices.why: Right: length extension, which HMAC's two passes prevent.

choices.text: It would be slower than HMAC
choices.why: It would be about as fast.

prompt: Why is the timestamp `t` placed inside the bytes the gateway signs, and not only in the header?
hint: What could somebody do to an unsigned field?

choices.text: So altering it breaks the tag
choices.why: Right: and so evt-3's old time cannot be refreshed.

choices.text: So the receiver can sort deliveries by time
choices.why: Sorting needs no signature.

choices.text: Because HMAC needs a number in its input
choices.why: HMAC takes any bytes.

choices.text: To make the tag longer
choices.why: The tag is 256 bits whatever goes in.

prompt: A handler parses the webhook JSON, logs the amount, then checks the HMAC tag with `==`. Which two changes matter most?

choices.text: Use SHA-512 instead, and a longer key
choices.why: The algorithm is fine.

choices.text: Log the body in full, and retry failed checks
choices.why: Retrying a failed check does not make it pass legitimately.

choices.text: Check the tag first, with a constant-time comparison
choices.why: Right: nothing from a stranger is read before the check.

choices.text: Accept only deliveries from the gateway's IP range
choices.why: Useful as an extra layer, not a replacement for the tag.

prompt: What is the namespace `-n file` for?

choices.text: It names the file being signed, for the record
choices.why: The file is given separately.

choices.text: It selects the key type
choices.why: The key decides its type.

choices.text: It compresses the signature
choices.why: Nothing is compressed.

choices.text: It ties a signature to one purpose
choices.why: Right: a file signature will not pass as a commit signature.

prompt: Five internal services verify login tokens. Today all share one HMAC key. What does switching to a signature, made by the login service alone, change?
hint: Who can mint a token in each design?

choices.text: Tokens become encrypted
choices.why: A signature hides nothing.

choices.text: Verification becomes faster than with HMAC
choices.why: Signature verification is slower than HMAC.

choices.text: Verifiers lose the power to mint tokens
choices.why: Right: signing and verifying become separate powers.

choices.text: Tokens no longer need an expiry
choices.why: They still do.

prompt: Which situations call for a signature rather than an HMAC? Choose all that apply.
hint: Who verifies, and who must not be able to produce?

choices.text: A firmware image checked by every device in the field
choices.why: Yes: devices must verify without being able to sign.

choices.text: A cookie issued and checked by the same server
choices.why: HMAC: the issuer is the verifier.

choices.text: An invoice a customer may dispute later
choices.why: Yes: a third party needs to know who signed.

choices.text: A gateway notifying a merchant it has a shared key with
choices.why: HMAC is the usual and sufficient choice.
